item.title: Best loan apps in Nigeria (2026): legitimate, low-interest options compared
item.dc:creator: Clinton Nwachukwu
item.description: Compare the best loan apps in Nigeria for 2026. See FCCPC-approved apps, real interest rates, loan limits and how to check a loan app is legitimate before you borrow.
item.content:encoded:
The best loan app in Nigeria is one that is approved by the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC), shows you the full repayment before you accept, and charges a rate you can afford. 

In October 2026 the FCCPC register listed 525 approved lending companies, alongside 112 apps on a watchlist and 54 delisted apps. So choosing a loan app starts with checking it is on the right list.

This guide compares popular loan apps in Nigeria, explains what their published rates mean in naira, and shows you how to confirm any app is legitimate.

Key takeaways

  • Check the company behind any loan app on the FCCPC register before you share your BVN.
  • Published rates vary widely, from under 36% a year to over 200% a year, so compare the total you repay, not the headline rate.
  • First-time borrowers get small limits. Larger amounts come after on-time repayments.

item.title: Tinubu ₦50,000 Grant: How to Check Eligibility and Receive the Government Payment
item.dc:creator: Daxonétété William
item.description: Find out how to check eligibility and receive Tinubu's ₦50,000 NERSI grant.
item.content:encoded:
Nigerians looking to receive the Federal Government’s ₦50,000 relief payment can now check the available beneficiary verification channels under the National Emergency Relief and Stabilisation Intervention (NERSI).

Announced on October 30, 2026, by the Minister of Humanitarian Affairs and Poverty Reduction, Dr Bernard Doro, the programme provides ₦50,000 to selected poor and vulnerable households across Nigeria.

Payments are being distributed through five approved providers: ALAT by Wema Bank, MoMo PSB, NairaGram, OPay and Moniepoint.

item.title: KrosAI is building the telecommunications infrastructure for voice AI in underserved markets
item.dc:creator: Chimgozirim Nwokoma
item.description: KrosAI is building the telecom infrastructure businesses need to deploy voice AI agents across Africa and other underserved markets.
item.content:encoded:
Joshua Firima has been building businesses since he was 16. His latest venture, KrosAI, wants to make it easier for businesses to deploy voice AI agents to communicate with customers, particularly in markets where the infrastructure needed to support them is not readily available.

Firima describes KrosAI as the AI-native telecommunications infrastructure enabling developers and businesses to deploy voice agents compliantly and reliably at scale in hard-to-reach markets.

It’s a long-winded description, but it, in some ways, mirrors how the startup arrived at its current business model.

The first version of KrosAI was a customer support agent designed to resolve queries. With companies increasingly exploring artificial intelligence in customer relationships, Firima wanted to build something businesses in Nigeria could use. But after moving to the United States in 2024, he realised that the problem he was trying to solve was largely addressed in more developed markets. The gap, he discovered, was in Africa.

item.title: Safaricom names Boniface Mungania as CFO
item.dc:creator: Justina Salami
item.description: Safaricom has confirmed Boniface Mungania as its Chief Financial Services Officer, effective November 1, 2026. He has held the role in an interim capacity since July.
item.content:encoded:
Boniface Mungania, OGW, has been confirmed as Safaricom’s Chief Financial Services Officer, effective November 1, 2026, according to a post by Mbugua Njihia, Safaricom’s advisor. Mungania has held the role in an interim capacity since July, when his predecessor left.

He brings close to two decades of experience across financial services, digital transformation, customer care and business development. 

He joined Safaricom in 2007 as a customer care representative. He later rose through several leadership roles, including Head of M-PESA Products and Services Development, Payments Tribe Lead and, most recently, Director of Public Sector Digital Transformation.

item.title: CBN’s new crypto rules put a ₦15bn price tag on issuing dollar stablecoins in Nigeria
item.dc:creator: Omoleye Omoruyi
item.description: Nigeria's new CBN rules set a ₦15bn minimum capital requirement for companies seeking to issue dollar-referenced stablecoins in the country.
item.content:encoded:
For a company hoping to issue a dollar-backed stablecoin to Nigerians, entering the market now requires a substantial financial commitment of at least ₦15 billion in paid-up capital, a Nigerian-incorporated entity, and sufficient readily accessible foreign currency to meet local redemption requests. The minimum liquidity threshold starts at $10 million.

The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) has also given existing virtual asset service providers 180 days to apply for the appropriate licences under its new Regulations for the Operations of Non-Security Virtual Assets in Nigeria, which took effect on November 5, 2026.

The rules cover stablecoins, deposit money tokens and related virtual asset services, including exchange, custody, transfers, payment processing and settlement. They establish a licencing and supervisory framework for businesses involved in these activities within or directed at Nigeria.

item.title: What it takes to place your first Temu order in Nigeria: A step-by-step guide
item.dc:creator: Daxonétété William
item.category: African e-commerce giant Jumia shares plunge as competition intensifies
item.description: Learn how to shop on Temu in Nigeria, choose products, make payments and track your first order from checkout to delivery.
item.content:encoded:
Temu has become an option for Nigerians looking to buy products from international online marketplaces, particularly as its catalogue of clothing, electronics, household items and accessories continues to attract shoppers.

Unlike shopping from a local retailer, buying from an international platform involves currency conversion, cross-border shipping, customs and local delivery arrangements. There are also questions about which Nigerian bank cards work, how long an order takes to arrive and what happens when a product is damaged or does not match its description.

item.content:encoded:
Ola Daramola, founder of Bluebulb, has had an interesting academic and professional trajectory. From acquiring a first-class engineering degree to years spent on large infrastructure projects to an entrepreneurial interest in solving problems.

item.title: Yellow Card acquires GoMoney to open direct operations in Brazil
item.dc:creator: Justina Salami
item.description: Yellow Card has acquired GoMoney, a Brazilian virtual asset service provider, to set up direct operations in Brazil. GoMoney’s full central bank authorisation is still pending.
item.content:encoded:
Stablecoin payments infrastructure provider Yellow Card acquired GoMoney, a Brazilian virtual asset service provider in October 2026. Financial terms were not disclosed.

The acquisition gives Yellow Card direct operations in Brazil, its first owned business in Latin America. 

GoMoney has applied to the Banco Central do Brasil (BCB) for authorisation to operate as a virtual asset service provider. The application falls under Law No. 14,478/2022 and BCB Resolution No. 519/2025. For now, GoMoney operates under Brazil’s transitional regime. Full authorisation still depends on the central bank’s review and approval.

The deal adds local collections and disbursements in Brazilian reais to Yellow Card’s offering. This includes payments through Pix, Brazil’s instant payment system, with settlement in stablecoins. The service will plug into the treasury and liquidity tools that Yellow Card already runs in its other markets.

item.title: CostGraph makes cloud costs easier to understand and manage. Now it wants to make it an infrastructure product
item.dc:creator: Chimgozirim Nwokoma
item.description: As AI drives cloud spending higher, CostGraph helps companies understand, optimise and automate their infrastructure cost usage across all dimensions.
item.content:encoded:
With artificial intelligence, building products has become significantly easier and faster. What has not become easier is tracking the cost of building them.

Imagine a technology company receiving a bill from its cloud services provider. The finance department can easily tell how much was spent, even if it cannot say precisely why. Meanwhile, the engineering team can look at the fine print to see which capabilities it used but may not immediately know the cost of each workload, application or customer. 

As technology companies spread their infrastructure across cloud providers, Kubernetes clusters and a growing collection of AI services, the distance between what a company consumes and what it pays for can become surprisingly difficult to bridge.

item.title: Chinese regulator questioned OPay before $304m US IPO withdrawal – report
item.dc:creator: Omoleye Omoruyi
item.description: A report suggests that regulatory inquiry from China may have influenced OPay to withdraw its planned NYSE IPO.
item.content:encoded:
A Chinese regulator made inquiries about OPay Limited shortly before the Nigerian-focused fintech withdrew its planned $304 million initial public offering (IPO) in the US, Bloomberg has reported, citing people familiar with the matter.

The report, published on Wednesday, November 4, offers the first indication of the country behind the regulatory inquiry that forced OPay to withdraw its proposed listing on the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE).

OPay had priced 16 million American depositary shares (ADSs) at $19 each on October 30, valuing the proposed offering at approximately $304 million and the company at about $4 billion. However, the shares never commenced trading after the company and its underwriters mutually terminated their underwriting agreement following the inquiry.
